title: JPMC SE III · Python Full Stack (practice)
description: Representative practice questions for a Software Engineer III Python full-stack loop: Python coding, Python internals, SQL, backend APIs, frontend, security, system design and behavioral. Modeled on commonly reported topics; not official or leaked questions.

questions.title: Two Sum
questions.prompt: Given a list `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indices `[i, j]` (with `i < j`) of the two numbers that add up to `target`. Exactly one answer exists. Aim for **O(n)** time.
questions.answer: Walk the list once and remember each value's index in a dict. For each `x`, check whether `target - x` was already seen. One pass, **O(n)** time and **O(n)** space. Mention the brute force (O(n²)) first, then optimize.

questions.title: Valid Parentheses
questions.prompt: Return `True` if the string of `()[]{}` brackets is balanced and correctly nested, else `False`. The empty string is valid.
questions.answer: Push opening brackets on a stack. On a closing bracket the top must be its partner, otherwise it is invalid. At the end the stack must be empty. **O(n)** time.

questions.title: Group Anagrams
questions.prompt: Group words that are anagrams of each other. Return a list of groups (any order).
questions.answer: Use a key that is the same for all anagrams: the sorted letters (`''.join(sorted(w))`) or a 26-letter count tuple. Collect words in a `defaultdict(list)` by that key. Sorting key: **O(n · k log k)**; count key: **O(n · k)**.

questions.title: Merge Intervals
questions.prompt: Merge all overlapping intervals `[start, end]` and return them sorted by start. Touching intervals (`[1,4]` and `[4,5]`) merge.
questions.answer: Sort by start. Keep a result list; if the next interval starts at or before the last end, extend the last end with `max`, otherwise append it. **O(n log n)** for the sort.

questions.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
questions.prompt: Return the length of the longest substring with all distinct characters.
questions.answer: Sliding window: remember the last index of each character. When you see a repeat inside the window, move the left edge to one past its previous index (never backwards, see `'abba'`). Track the best window size. **O(n)**.

questions.title: Top K Frequent Elements
questions.prompt: Return the `k` most frequent values in `nums` (any order).
questions.answer: Count with `collections.Counter`, then take the top k with `most_common(k)` (heap, **O(n log k)**). Bucket sort by frequency gives **O(n)**: index buckets by count, read from the highest bucket down.

questions.title: Design an LRU Cache
questions.prompt: Implement `LRUCache(capacity)` with `get(key)` (return value or `-1`) and `put(key, value)`. Both must be **O(1)**. When full, evict the least recently used key. `get` counts as a use.

tests.call: (lambda c: [c.put(1, 1), c.put(2, 2), c.get(1), c.put(3, 3), c.get(2), c.put(4, 4), c.get(1), c.get(3), c.get(4)])(LRUCache(2))

questions.answer: Use `collections.OrderedDict`: `move_to_end(key)` on every get/put and `popitem(last=False)` to evict the oldest. Interviewers often then ask for the manual version: a **hash map + doubly linked list** with sentinel head/tail nodes, so both lookup and reorder are O(1). Mention thread safety (a lock) if used across threads.

questions.title: Sliding-Window Rate Limiter
questions.prompt: Implement `RateLimiter(limit, window_seconds)` with `allow(timestamp) -> bool`. Allow a request if fewer than `limit` *accepted* requests happened in the last `window_seconds` (the window is `(timestamp - window_seconds, timestamp]`). Rejected requests are not recorded. Timestamps arrive in non-decreasing order.
questions.answer: Keep accepted timestamps in a `deque`. On each call drop timestamps `<= t - window` from the left, then accept if the deque is shorter than `limit`. Follow-ups: token bucket (smooth bursts, O(1) memory), per-user limits with a dict of deques, and a distributed version with **Redis** (`INCR` + `EXPIRE` for a fixed window, or a sorted set for a sliding window).

questions.title: Flatten a Nested Dictionary
questions.prompt: Flatten nested dicts into dotted keys: `{'b': {'c': 2}}` becomes `{'b.c': 2}`. An empty nested dict contributes nothing. Common when sending JSON config to a key/value store.
questions.answer: Recurse: for each key build `prefix + key`; if the value is a dict, recurse with that as the new prefix, otherwise store it. Mention recursion depth limits and an iterative stack version for very deep input.

questions.title: Write a Decorator
questions.prompt: Write a decorator `count_calls` that counts how many times a function is called in an attribute `calls`, and keeps the original function's name and docstring.

tests.call: (lambda f: (f(2), f(3), f.calls))(count_calls(lambda x: x * x))

questions.answer: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a wrapper. Use `functools.wraps` so `__name__`/`__doc__` are preserved (important for logging, Flask routes and debugging). Store state on the wrapper (`wrapper.calls`) or in a closure with `nonlocal`.

questions.title: Generator: Read in Chunks
questions.prompt: Write a **generator** `chunked(iterable, size)` that yields lists of up to `size` items. It must work on any iterable (including huge files) without loading everything into memory.
questions.answer: Use `yield` so values are produced lazily. Build a batch, yield it when full, and yield the last partial batch. Alternative: `itertools.islice` in a loop. In Python 3.12+ `itertools.batched` does this (yields tuples).

questions.title: Parse Access Logs
questions.prompt: Each log line ends with `"<METHOD> <path> HTTP/1.1" <status> <bytes>`. Return a dict of status code (as text) to count. Skip malformed lines.
questions.answer: Split from the right (`line.rsplit(' ', 2)`) to get status and size, validate the status is 3 digits, and count with a dict or `Counter`. For large files, stream line by line. A regex is fine too; say how you would handle bad lines (skip and count them, or log them).

questions.title: Net Balances from Transfers
questions.prompt: Given transfers like `{'from': 'A', 'to': 'B', 'amount': 50}`, return each account's net balance (money in minus money out).
questions.answer: One pass with `defaultdict(int)`: subtract from sender, add to receiver. Follow-ups they like in finance: use `decimal.Decimal` (never float) for money, validate negative/zero amounts, and make the operation atomic in a database transaction.

questions.title: GIL, threads, processes and asyncio
questions.prompt: What is the GIL? When would you use `threading`, `multiprocessing` and `asyncio`?
questions.answer:
- **GIL**: in CPython only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time. Threads still help for **I/O-bound** work because the GIL is released while waiting on network/disk.
- **threading / ThreadPoolExecutor**: many blocking I/O calls (HTTP, DB) with existing sync libraries.
- **multiprocessing / ProcessPoolExecutor**: **CPU-bound** work (parsing, number crunching); separate processes each have their own GIL. Cost: process start-up and pickling data.
- **asyncio**: thousands of concurrent I/O tasks on one thread with `async`/`await` (FastAPI, aiohttp). Never call blocking code inside a coroutine; offload it with `asyncio.to_thread`.
- Note: Python 3.13 has an optional free-threaded (no-GIL) build, still experimental.

questions.title: Mutable defaults, is vs ==, copy vs deepcopy
questions.prompt: What does `def add(item, items=[])` do wrong? What is the difference between `is` and `==`, and between `copy` and `deepcopy`?
questions.answer:
- Default values are evaluated **once** at definition time, so the same list is shared across calls. Use `items=None` then `items = [] if items is None else items`.
- `==` compares values (`__eq__`); `is` compares identity (same object). Use `is` only for singletons like `None`.
- `copy.copy` makes a new outer container that still points at the same inner objects; `copy.deepcopy` recursively copies everything.

questions.title: Classes, dataclasses and dunder methods
questions.prompt: Explain `@classmethod` vs `@staticmethod`, what `@dataclass` gives you, and what `__repr__`, `__eq__`, `__hash__` and `__enter__/__exit__` are for.
questions.answer:
- `@classmethod` receives the class (`cls`); good for alternative constructors (`from_json`). `@staticmethod` receives nothing; a plain function grouped in the class.
- `@dataclass` generates `__init__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__` (and ordering/frozen/hash options). Use `frozen=True` for immutable value objects.
- `__repr__`: developer-readable text. `__eq__`/`__hash__`: equal objects must have equal hashes to work in sets/dict keys.
- `__enter__`/`__exit__`: context managers (`with open(...)`, DB transactions, locks) that always clean up, even on exceptions. `contextlib.contextmanager` builds one from a generator.

questions.title: SQL: second-highest salary and top earners per department
questions.prompt:
Tables: `employee(id, name, salary, department_id)` and `department(id, name)`.
1. Return the second-highest distinct salary (NULL if none).
2. Return the top 2 earners in each department.
questions.answer:
```sql
-- 1
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM employee
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employee);

-- 2
SELECT department, name, salary
FROM (
  SELECT d.name AS department, e.name, e.salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.department_id ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employee e
  JOIN department d ON d.id = e.department_id
) ranked
WHERE rnk <= 2;
```
Explain `ROW_NUMBER` (no ties) vs `RANK` (gaps) vs `DENSE_RANK` (no gaps), and `INNER` vs `LEFT JOIN`.

questions.title: Indexes, ACID and isolation levels
questions.prompt: When does an index help or hurt? Explain ACID and transaction isolation levels with a banking example.
questions.answer:
- **Index**: B-tree that speeds up `WHERE`, `JOIN` and `ORDER BY` on its columns; composite indexes follow the left-most prefix rule. Costs: slower writes and more storage; low-selectivity columns rarely benefit. Check with `EXPLAIN`.
- **ACID**: Atomic (all or nothing transfer), Consistent (constraints hold), Isolated (concurrent transfers do not see half-done work), Durable (committed survives a crash).
- **Isolation**: Read Uncommitted (dirty reads) < Read Committed (default in Postgres) < Repeatable Read < Serializable. For a balance update use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` or an atomic `UPDATE account SET balance = balance - :amt WHERE id = :id AND balance >= :amt` to avoid lost updates.

questions.title: ORM N+1 queries
questions.prompt: An endpoint listing 100 orders with their customer names makes 101 queries. Why, and how do you fix it in Django and SQLAlchemy?
questions.answer:
Lazy loading fetches each order's customer in a separate query (1 + N). Fix by loading related rows up front:
- Django: `Order.objects.select_related('customer')` (JOIN for FK/one-to-one), `prefetch_related('items')` (second query for many-to-many / reverse FK).
- SQLAlchemy: `select(Order).options(joinedload(Order.customer))` or `selectinload(Order.items)`.
Detect it with query logging, django-debug-toolbar, or a test asserting the query count.

questions.title: Design a REST endpoint for payments
questions.prompt: Design `POST /payments` and `GET /payments` (with pagination) in FastAPI or Flask. Cover validation, status codes, idempotency, and error handling.

questions.title: Authentication and web security
questions.prompt: Compare session cookies and JWTs. How do OAuth2/OIDC fit in? How do you prevent XSS, CSRF and SQL injection?
questions.answer:
- **Session cookie**: server stores the session; easy to revoke. **JWT**: signed, stateless token; scales well but is hard to revoke, so keep it short-lived with a refresh token.
- **OAuth2** is for delegated authorization (access tokens); **OIDC** adds identity (ID token) for login/SSO, e.g. via an identity provider.
- Store tokens in `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, `SameSite` cookies rather than `localStorage` to limit XSS theft.
- **XSS**: escape output (React does by default; avoid `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`), Content-Security-Policy. **CSRF**: SameSite cookies plus CSRF tokens for cookie auth. **SQL injection**: parameterized queries / ORM, never string-format SQL.
- Also: least privilege, secrets in a vault (not code), input validation at boundaries, dependency scanning.

questions.title: React hooks and rendering
questions.prompt: Explain `useState`, `useEffect` (including cleanup and the dependency array), `useMemo`/`useCallback`, and why list items need a `key`.
questions.answer:
- `useState` holds component state; updates schedule a re-render. Use the function form (`setCount(c => c + 1)`) when the next value depends on the previous.
- `useEffect` runs after render for side effects (fetching, subscriptions). Deps array controls when it re-runs; return a **cleanup** function to unsubscribe or `abort()` a fetch, preventing leaks and race conditions.
- `useMemo` caches a computed value, `useCallback` caches a function identity; use them for expensive work or to keep props stable for `React.memo` children, not everywhere.
- `key` lets React match list items between renders; use a stable id, not the array index, when items can be reordered or removed.

questions.title: JavaScript event loop and debounce
Caching with Redis
questions.prompt: An account-summary endpoint is slow. How would you add caching, and what can go wrong?
questions.answer:
- **Cache-aside**: read from Redis; on miss load from DB, store with a TTL. On writes, update the DB then delete the key.
- Choose TTLs per data freshness; never cache data whose staleness breaks correctness (balances used for debits must come from the DB).
- Problems: stale data, **cache stampede** (many misses at once; use a lock or early refresh), memory eviction policy, and cache keys per user to avoid leaking data across users.
- Measure first: profile the query and add indexes before adding a cache.

questions.title: Testing with pytest
questions.prompt: How do you unit-test a function that calls an external payment API? Mention fixtures, mocking and what you would cover.

questions.title: Docker, CI/CD and cloud basics
questions.prompt: How would you containerize and deploy a FastAPI + React app? What does your CI/CD pipeline do?
questions.answer:
- Multi-stage Dockerfile: build React assets, serve them via Nginx or a CDN (S3 + CloudFront); a slim Python image running `uvicorn`/`gunicorn` as a non-root user.
- Config and secrets from environment / secrets manager, not baked into the image.
- **CI**: lint, type-check, unit tests, security/dependency scans, build image, push to a registry. **CD**: deploy to Kubernetes/ECS with rolling or blue-green deploys, health checks, and automatic rollback.
- Observability: structured logs, metrics, tracing, alerts.

questions.title: System design: real-time transaction alerts
questions.prompt: Design a service that sends customers a push/SMS/email alert within seconds of a card transaction. Millions of transactions per day; alerts must not be lost or duplicated.
questions.answer:
1. **Requirements**: latency (< 5 s), throughput, per-user preferences, at-least-once delivery with de-duplication, audit trail.
2. **Flow**: transaction service publishes `TransactionPosted` to **Kafka** (partitioned by account id for ordering) → alert service consumes, loads preferences (cached), applies rules (amount threshold, foreign merchant) → writes an `alert` row with a unique `(transaction_id, channel)` key → channel workers call SMS/email/push providers.
3. **Reliability**: idempotent consumers (unique key), retries with exponential backoff, dead-letter topic, outbox pattern so DB writes and events stay consistent.
4. **Scale**: add partitions and consumers, rate limit per provider, horizontal autoscaling.
5. **Ops**: metrics (lag, latency, failures), PII masking in logs, encryption in transit and at rest.

questions.title: Behavioral: ownership under pressure
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you handled a production issue or a tight deadline. What did you do, and what did you learn?
questions.answer:
Use **STAR**, about 2 minutes:
- **Situation**: one sentence of context and impact (who was affected, how badly).
- **Task**: your responsibility.
- **Action**: what *you* did, specifically: how you triaged, communicated with stakeholders, fixed, and verified. Say "I", not only "we".
- **Result**: measurable outcome (downtime reduced, defects avoided, deadline met) and the follow-up (post-mortem, monitoring, tests added).
Prepare 5 or 6 stories that cover ownership, conflict, failure, mentoring, and improving a process; JPMC interviewers often probe controls, risk, and doing the right thing for customers.

questions.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
questions.prompt: `prices[i]` is a stock price on day `i`. Buy once and sell once later. Return the maximum profit, or `0` if no profit is possible.
questions.answer: Track the lowest price seen so far; at each day the best sale is `price - lowest`. Keep the maximum. One pass, **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space.

questions.title: Product of Array Except Self
questions.prompt: Return a list where item `i` is the product of every number except `nums[i]`. Do it in **O(n)** without division.
questions.answer: Two passes. Left to right, store the product of everything before `i`. Right to left, multiply in the product of everything after `i`. No division, so zeros are handled naturally.
questions.solution:
def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = left
        left *= nums[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= right
        right *= nums[i]
    return out

questions.title: Number of Islands
questions.prompt: Grid cells are `'1'` (land) or `'0'` (water). Count islands: groups of land connected up, down, left or right.
questions.answer: Scan every cell. When you find unvisited land, count a new island and flood-fill all connected land (DFS with a stack, or BFS with a queue) so it is not counted again. **O(rows × cols)**. Prefer an explicit stack over recursion to avoid Python's recursion limit on big grids.

questions.title: Kth Largest Element
questions.prompt: Return the `k`-th largest value in `nums` (by sorted position, so duplicates count).
questions.answer: Keep a **min-heap of size k**: push each value and pop when the heap grows past k; the heap top is the answer. **O(n log k)**. `heapq.nlargest(k, nums)[-1]` does the same. Quickselect averages **O(n)**.

questions.title: Min Stack
questions.prompt: Implement `MinStack` with `push(x)`, `pop()` (returns the removed value), `top()` and `get_min()`, all in **O(1)**.

tests.call: (lambda s: [s.push(-2), s.push(0), s.push(-3), s.get_min(), s.pop(), s.top(), s.get_min()])(MinStack())

questions.answer: Store pairs `(value, minimum so far)` on one stack. Each push records `min(x, previous minimum)`, so the minimum is always at the top, even after pops.

questions.title: Reverse a Linked List
questions.prompt: Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head. `ListNode`, `from_list` and `to_list` are provided for testing; only write `reverse_list`.
questions.answer: Walk the list with `prev = None`. For each node: save `next`, point the node back at `prev`, then move `prev` and `head` forward. Return `prev`. **O(n)** time, **O(1)** space. Be ready to do it recursively too.

questions.title: Merge K Sorted Lists
questions.prompt: Merge `k` sorted lists of numbers into one sorted list.
questions.answer: Put the first item of each list in a min-heap as `(value, list_index, item_index)`. Pop the smallest, append it, push the next item from the same list. **O(N log k)** for N total items. `heapq.merge(*lists)` does exactly this lazily.
questions.solution:
import heapq

def merge_k_sorted(lists):
    heap = [(lst[0], i, 0) for i, lst in enumerate(lists) if lst]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    out = []
    while heap:
        value, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
        out.append(value)
        if j + 1 < len(lists[i]):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (lists[i][j + 1], i, j + 1))
    return out

questions.title: String Compression
questions.prompt: Compress runs of repeated characters: `'aabcccccaaa'` becomes `'a2b1c5a3'`. If the result is not shorter than the input, return the input unchanged.
questions.answer: Walk the string counting the current run; when the character changes (or the string ends) append `char + count`. Build pieces in a list and `''.join` them; repeated `+=` on strings can be slow.

questions.title: Roman Numeral to Integer
questions.prompt: Convert a valid Roman numeral (`I V X L C D M`) to an integer. A smaller symbol before a larger one is subtracted (`IV` = 4).
questions.answer: Map symbols to values. Walk left to right: if the next symbol is larger, subtract the current value; otherwise add it. **O(n)**.

questions.title: Missing Number
questions.prompt: `nums` holds `n` distinct numbers from `0..n` with exactly one missing. Return the missing number in **O(n)** time and **O(1)** extra space.
questions.answer: The sum of `0..n` is `n(n+1)/2`; subtract the actual sum. XOR of all indices and values also works and avoids overflow in fixed-width languages.

questions.title: Most Frequent Words
questions.prompt: Return the `k` most frequent words as `(word, count)` pairs. Ignore case and punctuation. Sort by count (high to low), then alphabetically for ties.

tests.call: top_words('the cat and the hat and the bat', 2)

questions.answer: Lower-case, extract words with a regex, count with `Counter`, then sort with key `(-count, word)`. For a huge stream use `heapq.nsmallest(k, items, key=...)` instead of a full sort.
questions.solution:
import re
from collections import Counter

def top_words(text, k):
    counts = Counter(re.findall(r"[a-z']+", text.lower()))
    return sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[:k]

questions.title: Meeting Rooms II
questions.prompt: Given meetings `[start, end]`, return the minimum number of rooms needed. A meeting ending at time `t` frees its room for one starting at `t`.
questions.answer: Sort by start. Keep a min-heap of end times of rooms in use. If the earliest-ending room is free by this start, reuse it (`heapreplace`); otherwise open a new room. The heap size is the answer. **O(n log n)**.

questions.title: Binary Search
questions.prompt: Return the index of `target` in the sorted list `nums`, or `-1` if absent. **O(log n)**.
questions.answer: Keep `lo..hi`; check the middle and discard the half that cannot contain the target. Watch the loop condition (`lo <= hi`) and the updates (`mid + 1`, `mid - 1`) to avoid infinite loops. In Python, `bisect` gives the same result.

questions.title: Coin Change (fewest coins)
questions.prompt: Return the fewest coins (unlimited supply) that make `amount`, or `-1` if impossible. See Chapter 5 of this app for a walkthrough.
questions.answer: `dp[x]` = fewest coins for `x`. `dp[0] = 0`; `dp[x] = 1 + min(dp[x - c])` over coins `c <= x`. Unreachable stays infinity, returned as `-1`. **O(amount × coins)**. Greedy (largest coin first) is wrong for sets like `[1, 3, 4]` and 6.

questions.title: Maximum Subarray (Kadane)
questions.prompt: Return the largest sum of a non-empty contiguous subarray. See Chapter 6 of this app for a walkthrough.
questions.answer: At each number, either extend the best run ending just before it or start fresh: `cur = max(x, cur + x)`. Track the best `cur`. Start from `nums[0]`, not 0, so all-negative input works. **O(n)**.

questions.title: Valid Anagram
questions.prompt: Return `True` if `t` is an anagram of `s`.
questions.answer: `Counter(s) == Counter(t)` in **O(n)**, or compare sorted strings in **O(n log n)**. Mention Unicode/case handling if asked.

questions.title: Deduplicate Transactions
questions.prompt: A feed may send the same transaction `id` more than once. Keep only the record with the highest `ts` for each `id`, and return them sorted by `id`.
questions.answer: One pass with a dict keyed by `id`, replacing the stored record when a newer `ts` arrives. In production this is an **idempotent consumer**: store processed ids (unique constraint) so redelivered events are ignored.

questions.title: Python memory management
questions.prompt: How does Python free memory? What are reference cycles, `__slots__` and `weakref` for?
questions.answer:
- CPython uses **reference counting**: an object is freed as soon as its count hits zero.
- A **cyclic garbage collector** (`gc` module) finds groups of objects that only reference each other.
- `__slots__` removes the per-instance `__dict__`, saving memory when you create millions of small objects.
- `weakref` lets you refer to an object without keeping it alive (caches, observers).
- Find leaks with `tracemalloc`; common causes are growing global caches and lingering references in closures.

questions.title: async/await in a FastAPI service
questions.prompt: When should a FastAPI endpoint be `async def` vs `def`? How do you call three downstream services concurrently?
questions.answer:
- `async def` when everything inside awaits (async DB driver, `httpx.AsyncClient`). Plain `def` endpoints run in a thread pool, which is safer for blocking libraries.
- Never call blocking code (requests, time.sleep, sync DB) inside `async def`; it freezes the event loop.
```python
async def summary(user_id: str):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=2.0) as client:
        acct, cards, alerts = await asyncio.gather(
            client.get(f'{ACCOUNTS}/{user_id}'),
            client.get(f'{CARDS}/{user_id}'),
            client.get(f'{ALERTS}/{user_id}'),
            return_exceptions=True,
        )
```
Say how you handle partial failure (timeouts, fallbacks, circuit breaker) and how FastAPI's `Depends` injects DB sessions and auth.

questions.title: Flask vs Django vs FastAPI
questions.prompt: When would you pick Flask, Django or FastAPI?
questions.answer:
- **Django**: batteries included (ORM, admin, auth, migrations); good for data-heavy apps and teams that want conventions.
- **Flask**: minimal and flexible; add only the pieces you need; good for small services.
- **FastAPI**: async, type hints with Pydantic validation, automatic OpenAPI docs; great for high-throughput JSON APIs and microservices.
The best answer ties the choice to the team, the existing stack and the requirements.

questions.title: HTTP methods, idempotency and status codes
questions.prompt: Which HTTP methods are idempotent? What is the difference between PUT and PATCH, and 401 vs 403?
questions.answer:
- **Idempotent** (same effect when repeated): GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS. **POST** is not, so use an Idempotency-Key for payments.
- **PUT** replaces the whole resource; **PATCH** applies a partial update.
- **401** Unauthorized = not authenticated (missing or invalid token). **403** Forbidden = authenticated but not allowed.
- Others: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable, 429 Too Many Requests, 500/503 server errors.

questions.title: SQL: self join and duplicates
questions.prompt:
1. `employee(id, name, salary, manager_id)`: list employees who earn more than their manager.
2. `person(id, email)`: find duplicate emails, then delete duplicates keeping the lowest id.
questions.answer:
```sql
-- 1
SELECT e.name
FROM employee e
JOIN employee m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

-- 2a
SELECT email FROM person GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- 2b
DELETE FROM person
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MIN(id) FROM person GROUP BY email);
```
Explain `WHERE` (filters rows) vs `HAVING` (filters groups), and run deletes inside a transaction after checking the count.

questions.title: SQL vs NoSQL and the CAP theorem
questions.prompt: When would you choose a relational database vs a NoSQL store? Explain CAP.
questions.answer:
- **Relational** (Postgres, Oracle): strong consistency, joins, transactions; the default for money and ledgers.
- **NoSQL**: document (MongoDB) for flexible schemas, key-value (Redis, DynamoDB) for fast lookups, wide-column (Cassandra) for huge write volumes, search (Elasticsearch).
- **CAP**: during a network partition a distributed system must choose **Consistency** or **Availability**. Banking ledgers choose consistency; a product catalog or activity feed can accept eventual consistency.

questions.title: Microservices and Kafka
questions.prompt: Monolith vs microservices? How does Kafka work, and how do you keep data consistent across services?
questions.answer:
- **Microservices**: independent deploys and scaling per team, at the cost of network calls, distributed failures and observability work. Start with a modular monolith when the team is small.
- **Kafka**: a durable log split into **topics** and **partitions**; order is guaranteed only within a partition (choose the key, e.g. account id). **Consumer groups** share partitions; offsets track progress.
- Delivery is usually **at-least-once**, so make consumers **idempotent**.
- Consistency across services: the **outbox pattern** (write the event in the same DB transaction, then publish) and **sagas** with compensating actions instead of distributed transactions.

questions.title: System design: URL shortener
questions.prompt: Design a service like bit.ly: create short links and redirect quickly at high read volume.
questions.answer:
1. **API**: `POST /links {url}` returns a code; `GET /{code}` responds with a 301/302 redirect.
2. **Codes**: base62 of an auto-increment or Snowflake-style id (no collisions), 7 characters gives about 3.5 trillion codes. Hashing needs collision handling.
3. **Storage**: key-value table `code -> url, owner, created, expiry`.
4. **Reads dominate**: cache hot codes in Redis or at the CDN; replicas for reads.
5. **Extras**: rate limiting, malicious-URL checks, analytics through an async queue, custom aliases, expiry cleanup.

questions.title: Object-oriented design: parking lot
questions.prompt: Design classes for a parking lot with several floors and spot sizes (small, medium, large). Vehicles park in the smallest spot that fits and get a ticket; fees are charged on exit.

questions.title: React state management and performance
questions.prompt: Context vs Redux vs React Query? How would you speed up a slow list of 10,000 transactions?
questions.answer:
- Local state first; **Context** for rarely-changing globals (theme, user); **Redux Toolkit / Zustand** for complex shared client state; **React Query / SWR** for server data (caching, retries, refetching).
- Slow list: **virtualize** it (react-window) so only visible rows render; paginate or infinite-scroll from the API; stable `key`s; `React.memo` rows; debounce filters; move heavy work off render with `useMemo` or a web worker. Measure with the React Profiler first.

questions.title: Cloud basics (AWS)
questions.prompt: Which AWS services would you use for a Python API with a React frontend? SQS vs SNS?
questions.answer:
- Frontend: **S3 + CloudFront**. API: **ECS/EKS** (containers) or **Lambda + API Gateway** (serverless). Data: **RDS/Aurora**, **DynamoDB**, **ElastiCache** (Redis). Secrets: **Secrets Manager**. Monitoring: **CloudWatch**.
- **SQS** is a queue: each message is processed by one consumer (work distribution, retries, dead-letter queue). **SNS** is pub/sub: one message fans out to many subscribers. Common pattern: SNS fan-out to several SQS queues.
- Use IAM roles with least privilege; no access keys in code.

questions.title: Code review, Agile and production support
questions.prompt: What do you look for in a code review? How does your team run sprints and handle production incidents?
questions.answer:
- **Review**: correctness and edge cases, tests, readability, security (input validation, secrets), performance hot spots, and consistency with team conventions. Be specific and kind; separate blocking issues from nits.
- **Agile**: sprint planning, daily stand-up, refinement, review and retro; small PRs with CI gates.
- **Incidents**: acknowledge, mitigate first (rollback or feature flag), communicate status, find the root cause, then a blameless post-mortem with action items.

questions.title: Behavioral: disagreement with a teammate
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate or manager on a technical decision.
questions.answer: Pick a real, professional disagreement (design choice, deadline versus quality). In STAR form: show that you **listened**, used **data** (a prototype, benchmarks, a risk list), escalated respectfully if needed, and **committed** to the final decision even if it was not yours. Finish with the outcome and what you would do the same or differently. Avoid stories that blame others.

questions.title: Behavioral: why JPMorgan Chase?
questions.prompt: Why do you want to join JPMorgan Chase, and why this team?
questions.answer: Make it specific and honest: scale and impact of the technology (systems that move money for millions of customers), interest in the line of business (Consumer & Community Banking, Corporate & Investment Bank, Asset & Wealth Management), the engineering culture (cloud modernization, reliability, security), and how your experience fits the role. Connect it to one or two things you researched about the team. Keep it under a minute.
